dimension: Online learning for cold-start identification of the best performers: bandits, best-arm identification, successive/sequential halving, Hyperband/ASHA, racing algorithms, sample-complexity lower bounds, non-stationary detection, and contextual bandits
citations_that_failed: FABRICATED QUOTATION. Beygelzimer, Langford, Ravikumar, "Error-Correcting Tournaments" (arXiv:0902.3176, full version, 1,293 lines of extracted text). The dimension attributes to it, in double quotes, the sentence that making every match redundant 2k-1 times yields "a regret ratio of at least log2 n, no better than the non-redundant single-elimination tournament". That sentence is not in the paper. There is no "Section on failed strategies". The nearest actual text is the intro claim that "Using multiple independent single-elimination tournaments is of no use as it does not affect the average regret of an adversary controlling the binary classifiers" -- a different claim about independent tournaments, carrying no log2 n bound. Worse, the paper says the OPPOSITE about repetition in its robust-search discussion: "Repeating the last comparison O(log k) times defeats this strategy." Under the founder's quote convention double quotes assert verbatim text, so this is the most serious defect in the dimension.

FABRICATED ATTRIBUTION. Same paper: "eliminating after k losses with arbitrary pairing also fails, an argument they note 'applies to a Swiss tournament'". The string "Swiss" occurs 0 times in arXiv:0902.3176. What the paper actually argues (intro, on m-elimination BRACKET tournaments) is: "the second-best player could defeat the first player in the first single elimination tournament, and then once more in the final elimination phase to win, implying that an adversary need control only two matches." That is about brackets, not Swiss pairing, and the paper makes no Swiss claim at all.

FABRICATED MEASUREMENT. "ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689) measured 3% to 6% of items as having negative discrimination." The paper exists and is correctly titled ("Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks", Li, Tang, Chen, Cheng, Metoyer, Hua, Chawla), but the string "negative discrimination" occurs 0 times in its full text. Its discrimination filter removes items with point-biserial r_pb < 0.1, and it reports no proportion. The 3-to-5 figure in the paper is an ITEM EXPOSURE rate: "Exposure values around 3-5% on HellaSwag and WinoGrande (for SE thresholds of 0.2 and 0.3)". An exposure statistic has been read as a discrimination statistic and its range widened from 3-5 to 3-6.

WRONG AUTHORS. "Hassidim, Kuperstein and Sharma, 'An Optimal Elimination Algorithm for Learning a Best Arm', NeurIPS 2020, arXiv:2006.11647". The actual authors are Avinatan Hassidim, Ron Kupfer, Yaron Singer. Two of three surnames are wrong (Kupfer not Kuperstein, Singer not Sharma). The title and arXiv ID are correct, and the attributed substance IS in the body -- the paper opens on "the constant terms hiding in the O notation" and states "in practice, there is a large gap between the sample complexity of our algorithms and MEDIAN ELIMINATION" -- so this is a citation-hygiene failure, not a substantive one.

MISNUMBERED. "Error-Correcting Tournaments (ALT 2009), Corollary 1: single-elimination has regret ratio at most ceil(log2 n)". arXiv:0902.3176 contains no Corollary 1. Its numbering is Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Corollary 3, Theorem 4, Theorem 5, Lemma 6, Theorem 7, Theorem 8, Lemma 9, Lemma 10, Theorem 11, Theorem 12, Lemma 13. The result claimed is Corollary 3: "reg(T(f),D) <= d reg(f,D')", where d is the depth of the tree -- which for a single-elimination tournament on n players is ceil(log2 n). The substance holds under a different label.

NOT VERIFIED IN THIS PASS (WebSearch budget exhausted mid-task; flagged, not refuted): ASHA (arXiv:1810.05934, MLSys 2020); Maron and Moore, Hoeffding Races, NIPS 1993; F-Race, Birattari et al., GECCO 2002; irace, Lopez-Ibanez et al., Operations Research Perspectives 3, 2016; Kandasamy et al., NeurIPS 2016; Even-Dar/Mannor/Mansour JMLR 7 (2006) 1079-1105; Lord 1971 flexilevel; Weiss 1973 stradaptive and its 9 difficulty strata; Birnbaum 1968; Kanarios et al. cost-aware BAI; "DCTAS". The HIGHEST-RISK item in this set is Waters (1975) and its figures 19.2, 26.5, 31.5 versus 48.4 items, because the dimension's "about a 2x saving, not 100x" verdict rests entirely on them and they sit in a 1970s psychometrics literature that is hard to reach. Treat that 2x as unconfirmed until the Waters paper is read.
overstated_verdicts: Sequential Halving: DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE is contradicted by the dimension's own text. Its transfers_to_cdsfl paragraph lists three breakages, one of which -- permanent elimination -- violates the HARD constraint that no model is ever permanently set aside, and a second of which -- synchronous rounds -- requires the central coordinator the founder has ruled out. A mechanism that breaks 2 HARD constraints by construction is APPLICABLE_WITH_CHANGES at best. The correct verdict is APPLICABLE_WITH_CHANGES, with the required change named: rolling re-admission (ASHA-style) plus asynchronous rung promotion.

Exponential-Gap Elimination: DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE is worse here than for Sequential Halving, because the dimension does not even flag the problem. Verified against the primary source: Algorithm 1 line 6 sets S_{r+1} <- S_r \ {i : p_hat_ri < p_hat_r* - eps_r}, an irreversible removal with no re-admission path. The entry's only caveat is about Median Elimination's constants. The no-permanent-elimination constraint is violated and goes unmentioned.

Mannor-Tsitsiklis lower bound: DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE is a category error. A lower bound is not a mechanism that can be applied; it is a constraint on mechanisms. The entry compounds this with "how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the cold-start budget", which is false -- the theorem gives an Omega with an unspecified constant, so it yields no budget (see quantitative_errors).

Beygelzimer et al. is treated as a result about model-ranking tournaments. It is a reduction from k-class classification to binary classification, in which "players" are class labels and "regret ratio" is multiclass regret divided by average binary regret. The transfer to "probability the best model is knocked out" is an analogy the paper supports only loosely (it does claim applicability to "tournament construction in games with real players"), and the dimension states it as a direct result.
quantitative_errors: 4x ERROR IN THE FIGURE THE DIMENSION ITSELF FLAGS AS MOST IMPORTANT. "The number that matters most to him: that system uses 52 to 101 items per model". Balkir et al. Table 2's own caption reads: "Items is the total number of items administered across the four hold-out models. % Used is Items divided by (4x Size)". The range 52+/-4 to 101+/-10, overall mean 87, is therefore the TOTAL ACROSS 4 MODELS. Per model it is 13 to 25, mean 21.75. The paper does contain a per-model figure, but it is a different one: at the unconstrained stopping rule it "would naturally fire at roughly 30-100 items per model depending on dataset", and the experiments ran at a budget of "the cost equivalent of 20 items per model". The verified floor against the founder's "2 or 3" is the hard minimum of 10 items per model, not 52.

THE LOWER-BOUND NUMBERS ARE COMPUTED OUTSIDE THE THEOREM'S STATED HYPOTHESES, WITH AN INVENTED CONSTANT. Mannor and Tsitsiklis, JMLR 5 (2004) 623-648, verified from the PDF. Theorem 1 reads: "There exist positive constants c1, c2, eps0, and delta0, such that for every n >= 2, eps in (0,eps0), and delta in (0,delta0) ... E_p[T] >= c1 (n/eps^2) log(c2/delta). In particular, eps0 and delta0 can be taken equal to 1/8 and e^-4/4". Theorem 5, the instance-dependent one, requires delta < delta0 = e^-8/8 = 0.0000419 and carries log(1/(8 delta)), not ln(1/delta), plus a constant c1 depending on p. Every number the dimension quotes -- 541, 2798, 1271, 139, and the per-model 48, 133, 300, 1198 -- was produced at delta = 0.05 with c1 set silently to 1. delta = 0.05 exceeds Theorem 1's delta0 by a factor of 10.9 and Theorem 5's by a factor of 1,192. eps = 0.25 and eps = 0.15 both exceed eps0 = 0.125. And log(1/(8*0.05)) = 0.916 against ln(1/0.05) = 2.996, a further factor of 3.27. The arithmetic is internally reproducible (I confirmed H1 = 1625/9 = 180.5556 and 180.5556 x ln(20) = 540.9 with SymPy exact rationals) but it is not a consequence of the cited theorem. The honest form is a SCALING law -- per-model cost constant in roster size, quadratic in 1/eps -- not "the floor nothing can get under", and it does not settle the 300-versus-3 dispute by arithmetic.

WRONG FORM OF THE LOWER BOUND. The dimension says Mannor-Tsitsiklis "[p]roves that for a wide variety of reward setups, ANY policy needs T = Omega(H log(1/delta)) pulls where H = sum_{i>=2} 1/Delta_i^2". Two errors. (a) The paper restricts to Bernoulli arms -- "Since we are interested in lower bounds, we restrict to the special case where each arm is a 'coin'" -- which is the opposite of "a wide variety of reward setups". (b) Theorem 5's sum is NOT sum_{i>=2} 1/Delta_i^2. It is c1 { (|M(p,eps)|-1)+ / eps^2 + sum_{l in N(p,eps)} 1/(p* - p_l)^2 } log(1/(8 delta)), where N(p,eps) excludes every arm within eps of the best (those contribute 1/eps^2 each via M) and also every arm with bias below a floor p. The quadratic-gap sum is over a restricted set, not over the roster.

MISSTATED DIRECTION OF A LOWER BOUND. "[P]roves no forecaster can achieve exp(-cn/H2) for all distributions", attributed to Audibert, Bubeck, Munos. Verified Theorem 4 (Lower Bound) reads: for any forecaster there exists a permutation such that e_n >= exp(-(5+o(1)) n / (p(1-p) H2)). That forbids beating the H2 rate; it does not forbid achieving it. The same paper states its own Successive Rejects algorithm achieves order exp(-n/(log(2K) H2)), i.e. the H2 rate up to log(2K). As written the claim contradicts the paper's headline result.

MILLER'S RESAMPLING NUMBERS ARE EXAMPLE-SPECIFIC AND THE QUALIFIER IS DROPPED. Verified: "Going from K = 1 (no resampling of answers) to K = 2, the total variance is reduced by 1/3. Increasing to K = 4, we have a variance reduction of 1/2 ... The upper limit on variance reduction via resampling in this example is 2/3." Those figures follow from Var(mu_hat|K) = Var(mu_hat|K=1) x (1 + 2/K)/3, which holds only under the paper's worked assumptions (binary scores, question difficulty x ~ U[0,1], giving Var(x) = 1/12 and E[sigma_i^2] = 1/6). The dimension states 1/3, 1/2 and the 2/3 floor as general facts.

THE 1,000-QUESTION HEADLINE IS QUOTED WITHOUT ITS EFFECT SIZE, AND THE EFFECT SIZE IS THE WHOLE POINT. Equation 9 and n = 969 verify exactly, as does "new evals should contain at least 1,000 questions". But 969 is the count needed to detect a 3-point difference at 80% power; the paper also calls its parameters "fictional". Inverting the same Equation 9 with the same omega^2 = 1/9 gives 349 questions at a 5-point effect, 87 at 10 points, 22 at 20 points and 10 at 30 points. For the founder's coarse tiering, Miller's own formula supports roughly 22 questions, not 1,000. Citing only the 1,000 figure in disagreement 3 overstates the requirement by a factor of about 44 at the effect size he actually needs -- and the dimension's own concession of a "10 to 300" honest range contradicts its own headline.

UNREPRODUCIBLE BECAUSE THE INPUT VECTOR IS NOT STATED (measured-rate-travels-with-its-script). "308,956 for 70 models with gaps spanning 0.05 to 0.60", "7,273,855 for 700 models with gaps from 0.02", and "6 models with one rival at gap 0.05 give T >= 1,271" cannot be recomputed: no gap vector is given. My closest reconstruction of the 6-model case (one gap at 0.05, four at 0.40-0.45) gives 1,269, so the figure is plausible, but it is a claim about evidence rather than evidence. Every other number I could reconstruct did check out: H1 = 1625/9 = 180.5556; Sequential Halving budget 24,926 at ceil(log2 5) = 3 (18,340 if exact log2 5 is used, so the ceiling convention is load-bearing and unstated); 2,798 and 559.6 per model; 139 and 27.8 per model; 48/133/300/1198 per model; round-0 allocation 0.4286 at n = 70 and 0.3000 at n = 700 (and exactly 1.0000 at n = 5, so T = 3n IS executable at the founder's actual roster size -- the infeasibility bites only at 70 and 700, which the dimension does say).

THE BINOMIAL ARITHMETIC IS CORRECT AND I CONFIRM IT. With SymPy exact rationals: 1 attempt gives 3/5 = 0.600 and 3 attempts give 1371/2000 = 0.6855 for 0.70 versus 0.50 with ties coin-flipped. For 95% correct ordering, SciPy gives exactly 32 attempts at 0.70/0.50, 134 at 0.60/0.50 and 540 at 0.55/0.50 -- so the dimension's 32, 134 and 540 all reproduce on the convention "hold p_b = 0.50 fixed and lower p_a", which it does not state. The normal approximation z^2(p_a(1-p_a)+p_b(1-p_b))/(p_a-p_b)^2 with z = 1.645 gives 31.1, 133.9 and 538.4, agreeing within 2 trials as claimed. Note the formula is labelled z_{alpha/2} but a correct-ordering requirement is one-sided, so z = 1.645 is right and the subscript is wrong.

missed_mechanisms.name: Top-m / subset identification (bandit subset selection, LUCB family)
missed_mechanisms.citation: Emilie Kaufmann and Shivaram Kalyanakrishnan, "Information Complexity in Bandit Subset Selection", COLT 2013, PMLR 30:228-251, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v30/Kaufmann13.html (verified: title, authors, pages, and that the problem is "efficiently exploring the arms of a stochastic bandit to identify the best subset"). The algorithmic ancestor is LUCB, Kalyanakrishnan, Tewari, Auer and Stone, "PAC Subset Selection in Stochastic Multi-armed Bandits", ICML 2012 -- NOT re-verified in this pass, cite with care.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the obvious specialist miss and it is structural, not marginal. The founder wants TIERS -- a partition of the roster into ordered bands. Every mechanism the dimension marks DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE (Sequential Halving, Exponential-Gap Elimination, Mannor-Tsitsiklis) solves single-best-arm identification, which returns one winner and says nothing about the ordering of the rest. Subset-selection bandits are the matching problem class: they identify the top m, they come with their own information-theoretic complexity characterisation, and the LUCB family samples only the 2 arms currently straddling the m-th boundary rather than eliminating anyone -- which satisfies the HARD constraint that no model is ever permanently set aside, the one constraint every mechanism the dimension did adopt violates by construction.

missed_mechanisms.name: Track-and-Stop and the exact fixed-confidence complexity constant T*(mu)
missed_mechanisms.citation: Aurelien Garivier and Emilie Kaufmann, "Optimal Best Arm Identification with Fixed Confidence", COLT 2016, PMLR 49:998-1027, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v49/garivier16a.html (verified: title, authors, pages, and that it gives "a complete characterization of the complexity of best-arm identification in one-parameter bandit problems" and "a new, tight lower bound on the sample complexity").
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: It repairs the dimension's single worst quantitative defect. The dimension computes numeric budget floors from a 2004 Omega bound whose constant is unspecified and whose delta0 is 0.0000419, then presents them as "the floor nothing can get under". The tight characterisation exists: the optimal sample complexity is T*(mu) log(1/delta) with T*(mu) given explicitly as the value of a max-min optimisation over arm-allocation weights, and Track-and-Stop attains it asymptotically. A specialist asked to settle a 300-versus-3 dispute would solve that optimisation for the founder's actual gap vectors and get a defensible number, instead of multiplying H1 by ln(1/delta) and hoping the hidden constant is 1.

missed_mechanisms.name: Non-stationarity detection and contextual bandits -- named in the dimension's own title, absent from its mechanism list
missed_mechanisms.citation: Not independently re-verified in this pass (WebSearch budget exhausted). The canonical anchors are Garivier and Moulines, "On Upper-Confidence Bound Policies for Switching Bandit Problems", ALT 2011 (discounted UCB and sliding-window UCB); the CUSUM-UCB / M-UCB change-detection line; and Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire, "A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation", WWW 2010 (LinUCB). Verify before citing to the founder.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension's own title promises "non-stationary detection, and contextual bandits" and the visible mechanism list delivers neither. This is not a pedantic gap. A vendor can silently re-point a model endpoint at a new checkpoint, so a seat's true ability is a drifting quantity. Every mechanism the dimension adopted assumes stationary arm means, and stationarity is exactly what breaks in a roster of hosted models. Worse, a drifting arm interacts lethally with permanent elimination: an arm eliminated in round 0 on a bad day can never be re-measured, which is both the HARD-constraint violation the dimension waves through and a live measurement error. The contextual half matters because model strength is task-class-dependent, which is also the premise of the dimension's own intransitivity worry in disagreement 4 -- it raises the problem and then omits the literature that addresses it.

missed_mechanisms.name: Decentralised / gossip multi-agent bandits for the no-central-coordinator constraint
missed_mechanisms.citation: Not independently verified in this pass. The relevant line is the multi-agent / gossiping bandit literature (for example Chawla et al., "The Gossiping Insert-Eliminate Algorithm for Multi-Agent Bandits", AISTATS 2020, and the Landgren-Srivastava-Leonard distributed-cooperative-decision line). Verify before citing.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The founder names "must work with no central coordinator" as a HARD constraint. The dimension's only distributed citation is Hillel, Karnin, Koren, Lempel and Somekh, NIPS 2013 -- which I verified does give a sqrt(k) speedup with one communication round, but which still aggregates at a central point after that round. Decentralised bandits, where agents exchange arm estimates over a graph with no coordinator, are the literature that actually matches the constraint, and the dimension does not reach it. Flagging this as unverified rather than asserting it.

notes:
BOTTOM LINE. The dimension's central thesis survives adversarial checking: the wheel is invented, and the three named precedents are real. I verified Karnin, Koren and Somekh (ICML 2013) line by line against the PDF -- Algorithm 2 IS called Sequential Halving, its allocation IS t_r = floor(T/(|S_r| ceil(log2 n))), Theorem 4.1 IS 1 - 3 log2(n) exp(-T/(8 H2 log2 n)), Theorem 3.1 and Algorithm 1's eps_r = 2^-r/4, delta_r = delta/(50 r^3), t_r = (2/eps_r^2) ln(2/delta_r) all match exactly, and the paper itself writes "T = O(H2 log n log(log n / delta))" in the form quoted. Audibert, Bubeck and Munos (COLT 2010) checks out on H1, H2, H2 <= H1 <= log(2K) H2, the Successive Rejects rate as "of order exp(-n/(log(2K) H2))" in the paper's own words, UCB-E's dependence on an unknown H1, and the paper's own admission that it could not prove a guarantee for adaptive UCB-E. Balkir et al. (arXiv:2601.13885v2) is real, correctly dated at v2 of 14 Sep 2026, and 9 of its 10 quoted figures verify verbatim including the cost-aware sentence "tests cheaper models to maximize uncertainty reduction per dollar spent", the 0.75 tau at 2% of budget, the 0.13 tau gain, 99% accuracy, 32% item reduction, 39% cost saving, the gamma = 0.95 pairwise threshold, the "minimum of 10 items per model before stopping", the 17 calibration models giving 68 configurations out of 21 models at 4 temperatures, and the break-even at "roughly 70 model evaluations on a dataset". The dimension found a genuinely close match to the founder's design and read most of it accurately.

WHAT MUST BE CORRECTED BEFORE THIS GOES TO HIM. Three items are blocking. First, the Error-Correcting Tournaments entry contains a double-quoted sentence that is not in the paper and a Swiss-tournament attribution with 0 occurrences of the word, and the paper's actual position on repetition in the robust-search setting is close to the opposite of what is claimed. Second, "ATLAS measured 3% to 6% of items as having negative discrimination" is an item-exposure statistic (3-5%) read as a discrimination statistic; ATLAS never mentions negative discrimination. Third, "52 to 101 items per model" is 4x too high -- Balkir's Table 2 caption states those are totals across 4 hold-out models, so the per-model figure is 13 to 25 with a mean of 21.75, and the real floor against "2 or 3" is the hard minimum of 10. Two further items are serious: every lower-bound number was computed at delta = 0.05 and eps up to 0.25, both outside the Mannor-Tsitsiklis hypotheses (delta0 = e^-4/4 = 0.00458 for Theorem 1, e^-8/8 = 0.0000419 for Theorem 5, eps0 = 1/8), with the unspecified constant set to 1 and log(1/(8 delta)) replaced by ln(1/delta); and the Hassidim paper's authors are Hassidim, Kupfer and Singer, not Hassidim, Kuperstein and Sharma.

WHERE I DISAGREE WITH THE DIMENSION'S VERDICT ON THE FOUNDER'S BUDGET. The dimension says "2 OR 3 SHOULD DO" IS REFUTED BY EXACT ARITHMETIC. I confirm the arithmetic -- 3/5 at 1 attempt, 1371/2000 at 3, 32 attempts for 95% ordering at a 0.20 gap -- but the arithmetic answers a question the founder may not be asking. It prices a GUARANTEED PAIRWISE ORDERING at 95% confidence. If what he wants is coarse tier assignment, Miller's own Equation 9 prices a 20-point effect at 22 questions, the eps-best-arm scaling prices eps = 0.25 at tens per model, and Balkir's measured system spends 13 to 25 per model with a floor of 10. The honest refutation of "2 or 3" is the factor of 4 to 10, not the factor of 100 the dimension's headline numbers imply. The dimension's own concession of a "10 to 300, instrument-dependent" range is the defensible claim, and it is buried under figures that overstate it.

THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL THING THE DIMENSION MISSED. It solves single-best-arm identification three ways and the founder's problem is ordered tiering. Subset-selection bandits are the matching class, and they also happen to resolve the HARD-constraint violation that every adopted mechanism carries: LUCB-style samplers never permanently eliminate an arm. Sequential Halving and Exponential-Gap Elimination both do, irreversibly, and the dimension marks both DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE anyway -- for Exponential-Gap Elimination without even flagging it.

METHOD AND REPRODUCIBILITY. Primary sources were fetched as PDFs and read as extracted text rather than summarised: Karnin ICML 2013, Audibert COLT 2010, Mannor-Tsitsiklis JMLR 5 (2004), Miller arXiv:2411.00640, Beygelzimer arXiv:0902.3176, Balkir arXiv:2601.13885v2, ATLAS arXiv:2511.04689, Hassidim arXiv:2006.11647, plus publisher pages for Jamieson-Talwalkar PMLR 51:240-248, Hillel NIPS 2013, Gharat arXiv:2609.30360, Garivier-Kaufmann PMLR 49:998-1027 and Kaufmann-Kalyanakrishnan PMLR 30:228-251. All arithmetic was cross-checked with 2 independent tools as required: SymPy exact rationals against SciPy/NumPy floating point for the binomial and H1/H2 figures, and they agree.
